name: Front Squat
tierNote: Safety tier A from content.md appendix B (spinal loading; high skill). census.json difficulty tier 1.
parentNote: Supervisor's LB4A brief names barbell_back_squat as the template parent. Same hand archetype (on-body) and primary contact (standing-feet), so the content.md 2.3 family rule holds. content.md appendix A had front_squat as a stand-alone parent; the brief overrides it.

inherit.field: setup[2] (load the plates evenly, collars on)
inherit.why: true for this child because it is the same straight barbell loaded the same way; nothing about plate loading depends on where the bar rests.

inherit.field: posture[3] (feet flat, knees follow the toes)
inherit.why: true for this child because Catalyst's front squat technique gives the same rule: whole-foot balance and knees in line with the feet (c10).

claims.text: The front squat emphasises an upright posture, a rigid trunk and quad strength.

quotes.text: The front squat is a more specific leg and trunk strength exercise to support the clean and jerk by emphasizing maximally upright posture, trunk rigidity and quad strength.

claims.text: The bar sits in the channel between the throat and the top of the shoulders, touching the throat lightly without pressing on it; slightly raised shoulders keep pressure off the collarbones.

quotes.text: Place the bar in the channel between the throat and the highest points of the shoulders.
The bar should be in light contact with your throat but not placing pressure against it, and the slight elevation of the shoulders will keep pressure off of your collarbones and carotid arteries.

claims.text: In a correct rack the shoulders hold the bar, pushed forward and slightly up (a shrug makes a shelf for it); the hands and arms only add security and should not do the main work, and a fingertip rack is fine if the bar stays on the shoulders.

quotes.text: It may also be beneficial to shrug the shoulders during the exercise; this creates more of a shelf for the bar to sit in.
The priority is the bar’s direct support by the trunk, so a fingertip rack position is preferable to a full grip with the bar not fully supported by the shoulders.
extend your upper back, and push your shoulders forward as far as you can and slightly up.

If the shoulder and bar positions are correct, the bar will remain secure without being held by the hands. The hands and arms provide added security, but should not be doing the primary work of holding the bar in place.

claims.text: Keep the hands wrapped round the bar as far as possible with a loose grip, elbows high, bar supported on the trunk.

quotes.text: Keep the hands wrapped around the bar as much as you can while keeping the elbows raised high and the bar securely supported on the trunk, but the grip loose.

claims.text: If a full grip is not possible, try other grip widths; a fingertip rack with the bar on the shoulders beats a full grip with the bar off them.

quotes.text: experiment with different grip widths
The priority is the bar’s direct support by the trunk, so a fingertip rack position is preferable to a full grip with the bar not fully supported by the shoulders.

claims.text: The bar can be held with a clean grip or with the arms crossed.

quotes.text: Stand in an erect position, holding the bar in either a clean grip or with the arms crossed.

claims.text: Keep the elbows high, or the bar may slip; the lift trains a tall chest and stops the habit of leaning forward.

quotes.text: Keep the elbows high during this exercise. If not, the bar may slip out of position. The purpose of this exercise is to keep the chest tall and break or prevent the habit of leaning forward.

claims.text: Heels about hip width or a little wider, toes turned out 15-30 degrees.

quotes.text: Place the heels at approximately hip width or slightly wider and turn the toes out 15-30 degrees from the center line.

claims.text: Brace the trunk hard with the lower back in its neutral curve and the upper back as flat as possible.

quotes.text: Pressurize and brace the trunk forcefully with the lower back in its neutral curvature and the upper back flattened as much as possible.

claims.text: Bend knees and hips together and squat straight down, balanced over the whole foot, knees in line with the feet.

quotes.text: Bend at the knees and hips together to squat as directly down as possible, maintaining even balance over the whole foot.
Keep the knees approximately in line with the feet.

claims.text: Depth: as deep as whole-foot balance and a neutral spine allow; one textbook excerpt stands up once the hip crease passes below the top of the knee.

quotes.text: Full depth is the knee joint closed as much as possible while maintaining whole foot balance and a neutral spine.
Once the crease of the hips goes below the crest of the knee, return to the starting position.

claims.text: Stay tight through the bottom and drive up keeping the torso upright and the whole foot down.

quotes.text: Maintain tension throughout the legs and trunk all the way through the bottom, and accelerate back up while maintaining an upright posture and whole foot balance.

claims.text: If you get dizzy, let a little air out as you stand, without losing the brace.

quotes.text: Release a small amount of air as you stand without compromising trunk rigidity if you need to avoid dizziness.

claims.text: Way out: set the safety bars just below your lowest depth (the source gives this height for the back squat and says the front squat is set similarly: inference); to bail, let go and let the bar drop forward onto them while stepping back.

quotes.text: Set the Safeties: Similar to the back squat, set the safety bars at an appropriate height.
quotes.where: How to Bail a Front Squat

quotes.text: Ensure your safeties or pins are set just below your lowest squat depth.
quotes.where: How to Bail a Back Squat

quotes.text: If you need to bail, quickly release the bar from your shoulders and let it drop forward onto the safety bars. Step back simultaneously to avoid any contact with the falling bar.
quotes.where: How to Bail a Front Squat

claims.text: Load progression: add load progressively within your limits; safeties are for emergencies, not a training method.

quotes.text: Proper training techniques, progressive loading, and knowing your limits are key to avoiding situations where you need to bail.
quotes.where: The Risks of Bailing a Squat

quotes.text: Safeties are for emergencies; they're not supposed to be a method of training.
quotes.where: The Importance of Spotters and Safeties

claims.text: In 15 trained people the front squat recruited muscle as well as the back squat, with lower knee compressive forces and extensor moments.

quotes.text: The front squat was as effective as the back squat in terms of overall muscle recruitment, with significantly less compressive forces and extensor moments.

claims.text: At maximal loads (n=12) the inner quad (vastus medialis) was more active in the front squat on the way up, and the back squat leaned the trunk further forward.

quotes.text: the electromyographic activity of vastus medialis was found to be greater in the front squat compared to the back squat during the ascending phase
Compared to the front squat version, back squat exhibited significantly greater trunk lean, with no differences occurring in the knee joint kinematics throughout the movement.

claims.text: Muscle targets named for the front squat: quadriceps, glutes (medius and maximus), tensor fasciae latae and hamstrings.

quotes.text: Muscle target: Quadriceps, gluteus medius, gluteus maximus, tensor fasciae latae, and hamstrings.

claims.text: A general review of resistance exercise (not front-squat data): holding the breath under heavy load raises intra-abdominal pressure, which may help trunk rigidity, and raises blood pressure; the health risk is unconfirmed.

quotes.text: The VM was associated with an increase in blood pressure during resistance exercise

the VM effectively increases IAP, which may assist with spine stability and trunk rigidity during resistance exercise. The health risks associated with the VM during resistance exercise remain unconfirmed.

claims.text: Some front squat training should be controlled through the deepest range, including pauses.

quotes.text: at least some front squat training should be done with control through the deepest range of motion, including pauses.

claims.text: NHS back pain: call 999 for pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in both legs, or bladder or bowel changes; see a GP if it does not improve after a few weeks.

quotes.text: Immediate action required: Call 999 or go to A&E if:
pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in both legs
changes in your bladder or bowels, such as difficulty peeing, or peeing or pooing yourself
it does not improve after treating it at home for a few weeks

claims.text: NHS knee pain: get advice from 111 if the knee is very painful, or locks, gives way or painfully clicks.

quotes.text: Urgent advice: Get advice from 111 now if:
your knee is very painful
your knee locks, gives way or painfully clicks – painless clicking is normal

claims.text: Lower-back feeling read as the torso tipping forward (inference): at maximal loads the more forward-leaning back squat was compared with the front squat, and the authors suggest the front squat may help prevent lumbar injury. The fix is the coaching cue: keep the elbows high and the chest tall.

quotes.text: back squat exhibited significantly greater trunk lean
the front squat may be preferred to the back squat for knee extensor development and for preventing possible lumbar injuries during maximum loading
Keep the elbows high during this exercise. If not, the bar may slip out of position. The purpose of this exercise is to keep the chest tall and break or prevent the habit of leaning forward.

claims.text: Have a spotter for heavy squats whenever possible; the source says to practise bailing with lighter weights (given in its back-squat section, applied here: inference).

quotes.text: Whenever possible, have a spotter when performing heavy squats.
quotes.where: The Importance of Spotters and Safeties

quotes.text: Practice this movement with lighter weights to get comfortable with the process.
quotes.where: How to Bail a Back Squat

claims.text: Walk out with one step back on each leg. Written for the back squat; applied to the front squat by inference (W2-R7).

quotes.text: Then walk back by taking one step back with each leg.

plate.viewWhy: The top fault (elbows dropping, chest falling forward, c7) and the upright torso (c1, c17) are sagittal; bar height on the shoulders reads from the side.
plate.equipment: Barbell in the front rack on the shoulders, rack upright with safety bars just below the bottom position (c14); floor line.
plate.start: Standing tall, bar in the channel between throat and shoulders (c2), elbows high with upper arms near level (c4, c7), heels hip width or a little wider, toes out (c8).
plate.end: Bottom: knees and hips bent together, torso upright, whole foot down (c10, c12), hip crease at or below the top of the knee (c11), elbows still high (c7).

checkpoints.label: Elbows high
checkpoints.what: Elbows stay raised so the shoulders hold the bar.

checkpoints.label: Chest tall
checkpoints.what: Torso stays upright down and up.

checkpoints.label: Whole foot
checkpoints.what: Balance over the whole foot, knees in line with the feet.

mistake.what: Elbows drop and the chest falls forward, so the bar rolls off the shoulders.
mistake.why: Human Kinetics: without high elbows the bar may slip out of position, and the lift exists to break the habit of leaning forward (c7).
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 2: the chest falling forward as the elbows drop (c7, c24) is the top fault. Harm: StrongLifts' squat page ties leaning forward to the lower back ("put your lower back at risk", "stresses your lower back"; written for the back squat, MECH) and lists "Leaning Forward" under its Common Issues; Yavuz ties the back squat's "greater trunk lean" to the front squat "preventing possible lumbar injuries" (c24, MECH); StrongLifts' front-squat paragraph says of low elbows "yours would most likely hurt if you try this without wrist wraps". Holding the bar up with the hands (c3) is tied to harm by one source, written for the back squat ("your wrists and elbows will hurt once the weight gets heavy", MECH), and is not on that list, so the chest wins the step-2 tie on the list and on the source count. Lower-back rounding is on the same back-squat list ("you’ll get hip pain" comes with knees pointing forward), and so is the knee cave ("Squatting with your knees caved in is bad for your knees", "will cause pain inside your knees"); each is tied to harm by one source (MECH), so the chest wins on source count, 2 to 1. Bailing with no safeties is a safeties choice, not a candidate. Set aside (no frequency word for a front-squat fault): StrongLifts' "most people lack the flexibility to Squat deep without their back rounding", "most people can’t keep their lower back neutral when they Squat deep", "Many people do partial Squats", "ass-to-grass or your lower back will usually round" and the ass-to-grass "Your lower back will most likely round at the bottom" are about the back squat (and "most likely" is a likelihood, not a frequency word); "Many strong Squatters look up during Squats and seem to be fine", "it usually means your Squat form is wrong", "The Buttwink is usually just lower back rounding" and "Most people don’t have the hip flexibility" are about the back squat; "Most people set them too high" is a rack setup choice and "Most people don’t know how to spot" a spotter choice; "Bodybuilders also often Front Squat" names no fault; Hackett's "often advised to avoid the VM" is about all resistance training; the NHS pages' "very common" and "often during exercise" lines name no fault of this exercise; rep-fail's "Regularly bailing can damage your equipment" is about equipment. Under D-SUP-PROTECT, rep-fail's "Protect Your Back: Always maintain a neutral spine and avoid twisting or bending awkwardly when bailing" is about the bail, no fault named on this card, and StrongLifts' "protects it against injury" lines name benefits, so they are set aside. handlingMistakes gains the top fault at [0] (R-LB2-2); bar pressing on the throat leaves the list under the cap of 3 (no harm word; risks[2] and feel.rows[2] keep it). The side view shows the chest and elbows, so drawable is true.

tells.text: Bar rests on your shoulders, hands loose
Elbows stay up out of the bottom

tempo.text: Controlled descent, drive up; some sets with control and pauses at the bottom (c21). No source gives seconds for the standard rep. The anchor lists variations, among them "a pause in the bottom" and "slow eccentrics (usually 3-6 seconds)"; these are options, not the default rep, so up, down and pause stay null (LR-33).

grip.type: Clean grip: full grip on the bar kept loose (c4); crossed-arm grip is an option (c6).
grip.width: No fixed width; try different widths until a full grip fits (c5).
grip.thumb: Wrapped as far as the rack allows; a fingertip rack is acceptable when the bar stays on the shoulders (c5).
grip.handContact: Bar rests on the shoulders, not in the hands; the hands only add security (c3).
grip.wrist: Front-rack exemption from the on-body 0-15 degree range, reason: the shoulders carry the bar and the hands only add security, and a fingertip rack is acceptable when a full grip does not fit (c3, c5). No source read gives a wrist angle.

setup.step: Set the safety bars just below your lowest squat depth.
Bar between throat and shoulders. Shoulders pushed forward and slightly up.
Heels hip width or a little wider, toes out 15-30 degrees.
Walk out one step back on each leg. Brace hard each rep.

posture.point: Bar in the channel, no pressure on the throat.
Knees and hips bend together, straight down.
Whole-foot balance, knees in line with the feet.
Depth as far as a neutral spine and whole-foot balance allow.
Torso upright on the way up.

handlingMistakes.fix: Keep the elbows high and the chest tall.
Push your shoulders forward and up. Try a fingertip rack.
Set the safeties. To bail, drop the bar forward and step back.

rows.means: The hands are holding the bar up.
rows.fix: Push your shoulders forward and up. Try a fingertip rack.
Keep the elbows high and the chest tall.

rows.means: Bar too far back or shoulders not up.
rows.fix: Raise your shoulders slightly so the bar only touches lightly.

rows.where: Very painful, locking or giving-way knee

risks.risk: A failed rep with no safeties set.
Holding your breath under heavy load raises blood pressure.

redFlagNote: back is the proposed new shared box (content.md 5.3); nhs-back supplies its triggers (c22). The wrist box text is the existing shared NHS box; this card only links it.

zooms.right: Bar on the shoulders, loose grip, elbows high.
zooms.wrong: Bar held in the hands, off the shoulders.

zooms.right: Arms crossed over the bar, elbows high.
Chest tall, elbows high at the bottom.

libraryDiff.why: Library: quads primary, glutes secondary. Yavuz 2015 (c17) supports quads as the main mover; Human Kinetics names glutes and hamstrings (c18). Hamstrings not added: the only EMG source found shows the hamstring muscle more active in the back squat, so no data supports it as a front squat mover. No change.

loadProgression.text: Add load progressively within your limits. Safeties are for emergencies.

wayOut.text: Safeties just below your lowest depth, or a spotter when heavy; practise bailing with light weight first. To bail, let go, let the bar drop forward onto the safeties, and step back.

breathing.text: Brace before each rep; release a little air on the way up if dizzy. Shared breath-holding line applies.

barPath.text: The bar sits in front of the throat, touching lightly, never pressing (clear of the neck).

anchorNote: Catalyst Athletics front squat page read in full; Catalyst clean rack position and Human Kinetics front squat excerpt also read in full.
unsourced: Rack hook height for the front squat (parent's line is back-squat specific, so it is not inherited).
A wrist angle for the front rack.
Knees caving (front view): StrongLifts names it for the back squat only; no front-squat source names it.
